Too deep for a cantilever wall: Without other support, embedded walls are stable only for excavations of a few metres (max. 4–6 m). An anchor, a strut or a slab is needed!
As a cantilever, max. 4–6 m – and only if there is no structure right beside it. See how much one anchor reduces the embedment and the moment!
The wall is fixed by the passive earth resistance; it rotates about a point near the toe (point C). d = 1,2·d₀ = ${fmt(r.d, 1)} m.
A shorter wall, but a larger span moment: the toe can move slightly, the wall works “as a beam on two supports” (anchor + passive earth resistance).
A longer wall, but a smaller span moment: the fixity of the toe creates a negative moment. The point of zero moment is about ${fmt(r.x, 2)} m below the bottom of the excavation.

A deep excavation has to be supported at several levels: the support forces here come from Peck’s apparent earth pressure, by tributary area – the real distribution also depends on the construction stages.

The force is transferred from the wall to the anchor through the anchor head. A bearing plate placed on the wall sets the direction of the anchor; the strands are gripped by conical wedges in the wedge plate.
One anchor supports several wall elements (piles, sheet piles, diaphragm wall panels) along the load-spreading waling.

Allows movement, no force is transferred to the soil: it carries the force between the head and the fixed length. A high-strength Dywidag bar or, most often, steel strands in a sheath; the bore is filled with cement grout. At least 4 m.
The possible slip surface of the retained soil mass. The fixed length has to start beyond it – otherwise the anchor would move together with the moving soil mass.
This is where the force is transferred: the grout body transfers the force to the soil by shaft shear. Typically 4–9 m long, extending beyond the active slip surface.

Typically 3–7 strands (depending on the force to be taken). A single Ø15,7 mm strand has a breaking force of about 279 kN (≈ 28 t) – five of them can already carry more than 100 t. Along the fixed length, spacers keep them apart.
A valved (sleeved) pipe running beside the strands: the high-pressure (post-)grouting is done through it, cracking and widening the primary grout body.

The slip surface is drawn from the bottom of the excavation at an inclination of 45° + φ/2 (a simplification). The free length has to extend beyond the slip surface by at least max(1,5 m; H/5), and be at least 4 m. Illustrative – the actual length comes from the pull-out resistance and the deep slip surface (Kranz) check.
Neighbouring building with a basement (−3,5 m)
The anchor is longer than 30 m – anchors are made at most 25–30 m long. Several rows of anchors or another support are needed.
Anchor length over 25 m – close to the practical limit.
The fixed length is typically 4–9 m; above 9 m the resistance hardly increases.
Anchors are typically inclined at 15–30° to the horizontal.
The anchor runs into the neighbour’s basement! A steeper anchor, a deeper anchor row – or a tubular strut is needed.
The anchor reaches ${fmt(over, 1)} m under the neighbouring plot – a legal issue (owner’s consent), and it can run into existing structures.
The fixed length starts beyond the slip surface, and the anchor stays on your own plot.

The strut buckles! A larger diameter / wall thickness, better steel, a shorter buckling length (intermediate support) or closer strut spacing is needed.
Above 25–28 m intermediate support is needed.
${fmt(sL.v, 1)} m: assembled by splicing transportable elements (typically 12 m, in special cases 14–18 m).
The additional force from temperature is ${fmt((c.dN / c.Nb) * 100, 0)}% of the resistance – a strut longer than 10–15 m has to be designed for it.
The strut safely carries the force from earth pressure and from warming as well.
A city-centre street: a multi-level structure will be built below the surface (underground car park, metro station, underpass).
First the retaining structures are built – diaphragm wall or pile wall – from the surface. Traffic only has to be diverted for this time.

If there are intermediate supports, their foundations (bored piles, barrettes) are made from the top, and the columns are placed: the steel column is lowered into the fresh concrete. In Hungary a temporary steel column is typically made beside the permanent columns.

After about 1–2 m of excavation, the top slab is cast on ground formwork (lean concrete + membrane) – without falsework. As a diaphragm it supports the walls; a muck-out opening is left in it, and the surface can be reinstated.

The further levels are excavated under the slab by mining methods, with small machines; the soil leaves through the opening, a transport tunnel or a “pocket”. The intermediate slab is also cast on the ground.
After the full excavation and the slabs are complete, the base slab is made; the columns are encased in concrete. No temporary struts or anchors were needed.
guide frame – the steel column is lowered into the fresh concrete
traffic diversion – only while the walls are built

Placement rule: the active wedge of the main wall and the passive wedge of the anchor wall must not overlap. Here we draw planes at 45° + φ/2 from the toe of the main wall and at 45° − φ/2 from the bottom edge of the anchor wall (a simplification on the safe side). The movement is illustrative, exaggerated.
Typically 0,8–1,0 m below the surface, in a narrow trench.
The anchor wall is in the right place
The anchor wall is inside the active wedge – no resistance
The two slip surfaces meet at ground level at most: the full passive wedge can develop in front of the anchor wall. Without prestress the wall moves a few cm before the rod becomes taut.
The passive wedge reaches into the moving soil wedge of the main wall. Move the anchor wall back to at least ${fmt(Lmin, 1)} m – or a deeper, shorter anchor wall is needed.
The anchor wall moves together with the soil: the rod gets no resistance. In the wrong place an anchor wall is worth nothing!
